From Kwong Fuk to Wang Fuk – A Home Chosen with Utmost Care

In February this year, the government announced a proposal to acquire the seven blocks of Wang Fuk Estate. By the end of June, it revealed that Wang Chi House, which had escaped the fire, would also be included in the acquisition. The entire estate will be demolished in the future and rebuilt as public facilities. Officials also said the primary principle of the acquisition is to be "tempered with compassion, reason and the law," with "compassion" taking precedence.

Compassion is an abstract concept, usually manifested through words and actions. After the disaster, Mrs. Tam passes by Wang Fuk Court every day and takes photographs. Her affection for the Kwong Fuk–Wang Fuk community dates back to her childhood—she grew up in Kwong Fuk Estate. After marriage, she tried to find a new home elsewhere in Tai Po but failed to find one. Her husband, who loved the sea, boldly declared he would buy a sea-view flat. To their surprise, the estate agent did find a unit in the nearby Wang Fuk Court.

Bought despite low bank valuation; moved in on the 10th handover anniversary

Mr. Tam said buying a home is a matter of feeling. That night, they viewed the flat at 11 pm. "The moment we stepped into the lobby with air-conditioning, it already felt wonderful." Nearly every window of the unit faces the sea; under the moonlight, Tolo Harbour shimmered, a gentle breeze rustled the trees, bringing a sense of peace. "The agent said others would come to view it the next day. The owner said if we put down a deposit on the spot, the flat would be ours." Mr. Tam hurried downstairs to withdraw cash, and by 1 am they had signed the provisional agreement with the owner.

It was 2007. Others said the unit was not worth more than a million, and the bank's valuation was also insufficient, yet the Tams remained devoted and determined to buy. Coinciding with the 10th anniversary of the handover, there was a rare fireworks display at the Handover Tower opposite their unit. They excitedly invited relatives and friends to their yet-to-be-renovated new home to watch, and even took their wedding photos at the waterfront park, full of hope for the future.

Estate garden reveals deep community bonds

After their son Oscar was born, the small family's ties with the community grew even closer. Neighbours on the same floor kept their wooden doors open; whenever the children heard Oscar coming home, they would run out to invite him to play. The estate has a garden called "Lok To Garden" for residents to grow plants, which is so popular that there is a ballot to decide who gets to use it. Mrs. Tam laughs that they reaped what they did not sow—because warm-hearted neighbours often helped water the plants and notified them when vegetables were ready to harvest. "Neighbours would call and ask, would you mind if I plant some kale at your plot? Of course we don't mind!" Their son loved seeing the sun rise just before school. After dinner, the family would stroll to the park to let off steam; on holidays they would cycle along the river and the sea. These are all cherished memories.

Mutual protection among neighbours; belief that "we can return home soon"

On the day of the fire, Mrs. Tam rushed home from the office with a neighbour she knew. That neighbour's mother was trapped in the fire, and they were frantic with worry. They could only break through the cordon to ask for information, and then there was nothing more they could do. Mrs. Tam then began contacting neighbours non-stop to confirm everyone's safety, reporting the number of occupants in each flat to police officers, and reconfirming every hour. "It was chaotic—everyone was jotting things down on A4 paper. I even asked the police if they could open an extra queue to help. It was just writing things down, yet they had to find the Care Team before opening another queue."

In the days that followed, the Tams accompanied their friend back and forth to the community hall, searching for her mother's whereabouts, giving directions to members of the public who spontaneously brought supplies to the scene, and helping distribute them. "My mental state was such that I couldn't even return to work, but we hadn't lost absolutely everything." Mr. Tam said the priority at the time was "comforting one another first, protecting one another together," and at that point both firmly believed they could return home soon.

Lingering questions; estimating that Wang Chi House alone can house unwilling owners for resettlement

However, hopes were dashed time and again. They thought that since Wang Chi House was undamaged, residents would be free to come and go. "Who would have thought that it wasn't until May that we could go upstairs again—such a thing could never happen in Hong Kong." Initially, the government's questionnaire mentioned options including rebuilding on the original site or at the park opposite, so they assumed there was hope of staying. Yet just two months after the fire, the government announced there would be no rebuilding. They then thought that at least Wang Chi House could be preserved, but in the end everyone was urged to sell their title, bidding Wang Fuk Court farewell forever.

Alongside disappointment, questions piled up. Yuen Chau Tsai Lane next to Wang Chi House was undamaged, and Mrs. Tam could not understand why they could no longer return home via the same road: "Why are we being restricted from going back to a building that is fine?" Mr. Tam noted that the government had previously said leaving Wang Chi House on its own would raise issues of repair and maintenance costs, shared management fees, and deed restructuring. But now that the government has become the major owner, negotiation should in theory have become easier. Based on government figures, he estimates that about 10% of owners are unwilling to sell, and the 248 flats in Wang Chi House would be just enough to accommodate them.

"I cannot think of any reason to give up for now" The government's acquisition deadline of 31 August is fast approaching, with over 90% of owners having accepted the buyout. Deputy Financial Secretary Wong Wai-lun has stated that if legislation is required for the government to compulsorily acquire the titles, property values would certainly drop significantly. Others say "it's only a matter of time," but the Tams have still not signed the letter accepting the acquisition proposal. "I cannot think of any reason to give up for now." Mrs. Tam has recently been receiving a steady stream of "reminder" text messages from explainers and admits the pressure is mounting. Yet what weighs on her is not just her own property, but the entire Kwong Fuk–Wang Fuk community.

"From day one, what you are doing is destroying the future of Kwong Fuk Estate. This insistence, beyond simply loving our home, is also about protecting the neighbours who are still waiting for justice... We are giving a little of our strength to protect Wang Fuk Court, and to safeguard the answers everyone is truly waiting for. If everyone gave up so easily, the matter would have been wrapped up long ago."

Repair could save HK$900 million; urges better use of public funds for Hong Kong

Looking at the bigger picture, she points out that acquiring Wang Chi House alone would cost one billion dollars, whereas choosing to repair it could save at least HK$900 million of public funds. "Redirect that HK$900 million to building Hong Kong's future—put it into education. Children are Hong Kong's future. I don't want you to spend HK$900 million demolishing a building that is safe to live in."
